speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am glad that both growing the economy and upholding fiscal prudence and fiscal responsibility are also featured in the Forward Singapore report.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a strong and vibrant economy creates good jobs and gives us the means to tackle social challenges and enables us to bring about better lives for our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Forward Singapore report also reminded us that we are stewards of our limited resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Where we in this House have committed not to dip into our Reserves set aside for future generations, outside of exceptional circumstances, we must ensure that we spend public resources prudently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But prudence does not mean incurring the lowest possible cost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure most Members would agree with the Building and Construction Authority’s (BCA's) and Ministry of Manpower’s (MOM's) decision to raise the weighting of safety-related criteria in the evaluation of construction tenders from 1 April 2024.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides after-the-fact audits by the Auditor-General’s Office and scrutiny by Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee, how does MOF ensure effective and prudent use of public resources?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The threshold works, for example, to exempt some small and medium enterprises (SMEs), such as hawkers and retail shops in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also helps avoid incurring additional costs to comply with GST accounting and collection requirements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost 30 years later, this figure of $1 million remains in place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In an earlier Parliamentary Question to MOF on this matter, it replied that the Ministry would continue to assess the appropriateness of this threshold as part of its regular policy reviews.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, are there plans to further simplify the compliance costs of GST registration, particularly for small businesses?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This has remained the case for many years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even though the effective tax rate of 2% is in place for those earning between $20,000 to $30,000, a figure that comes up to $200, this amount is not insignificant, especially for low-income earners, much of whose salaries get spent on food and consumables.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An additional $200 to spend on such items can provide much respite and support for some families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who rent HDB flats under the rental housing scheme, and at the lowest tier, $200 can pay for seven months of rent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry be able to share how it determines the circumstances it takes into account in deciding when to raise its chargeable income threshold for the first $20,000, either to increase it, in view of rising prices and inflation?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It establishes Singapore as a leading global hub for innovation and intellectual property development, ensuring a sustainable competitive advantage for businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given these goals, there is scope to expand our IP protection.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, cost of living remains as a top concern on Singaporeans' minds.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thus, I wish to seek the following clarifications, please.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government must continue to safeguard Singaporeans against profiteering.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am particularly concerned about our seniors' ability to afford and access at least sufficient and adequate nourishment, whether they dine at home or outside.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thirdly, how else would the Government assist Singaporeans with household expenses, such as from water and electricity consumption?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This point is raised as an aside to encouraging and incentivising households to minimising consumption levels.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fourthly, will the Government consider providing more support to social enterprises that provide free food to low-income families, especially those living in Housing and Development Board (HDB) rental flats, such as by giving matching grants to social enterprises?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The measures under Budget 2024 are commendable and under which everybody will receive a slice of the pie.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can we raise greater awareness so that every Singaporean understands the nature and extent of the assistance or relief that they will receive?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Simply put, the measures must not only work but also be felt by Singaporeans to be working.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairperson, we as a House and the Government have always worked to ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my view, it is our duty to ensure that Singaporeans are aware and assured that we have been and always will do our best for our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I look forward to the Government's response to my aforementioned points.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, in the 1970s, MOF provided the House with detailed breakdowns of the fees and taxes collected.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we know that in 1972, the Government collected about $190,000 in car park fines.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The information provided today is much less detailed in comparison.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why does MOF not provide a breakdown of these taxes, given the sizeable amount?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the estimated amount of levy collected for Work Permit, S Pass and Migrant Domestic Workers respectively in 2023 and 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the account code for ERP revenue and what was the estimated amount collected?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the reasons for the significant increase in corporate income tax from 2022 to 2023 of about $5 billion?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is there a significant estimated increase in property tax collected for private properties of $753 million in 2024 despite the upward revision of the Annual Value bands announced in Budget 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why is there a big estimated increase in land sale revenue from $18 billion in 2023 to $31 billion in 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much has been disbursed to SPH Media Trust in 2023 and how much estimated for 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the HDB deficits for 2023 and 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much was spent by Ministers travelling overseas to fulfil the obligations of their international appointments in their private capacity in 2022 and 2023?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many ongoing development projects have cumulative investment of more than $1 billion?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many projects with total investments of more than $1 billion are expected to be initiated in 2024?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) welcomes the Government’s efforts to support the retirement and healthcare needs of younger seniors through the Majulah Package.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But how do we know whether we have set aside too much?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister explain whether this means that too much money was initially set aside when the Merdeka Generation Fund was set up?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If yes, what will happen to the excess funds?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, in Budget 2024, as in previous Budgets, funds are allocated to support Singaporeans, reinforce our competitive advantage, build on existing strengths as well as upgrade sectors where we have competitive advantage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: An example of these funds is the top-up of the Financial Sector Development Fund by $2 billion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These initiatives are longer term and span over a few years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What measures does MOF take to assess and ensure the appropriate, effective and prudent use of public resources as they would be expected to be expensed over multi years?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, a resident, who is a single father taking care of two daughters in their early teens, shared with me that while he welcomed the change in law last year doubling the paternity leave from two to four weeks, the benefits which he received are significantly less than single mothers, divorced or otherwise, who are having care of their children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, he does not enjoy the substantial reliefs which a woman is entitled to under the Working Mother’s Child Relief.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My resident, who has a full-time job, would like to engage a migrant domestic worker to help with housework and care for his children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, he is not entitled to any tax relief under the Foreign Domestic Worker Levy Relief.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: IRAS allows women who are married, separated from their husbands, divorced or widowed, and had children who lived with them to claim the relief.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government consider equalising the entitlement to this relief, such that men or women can qualify to apply for this relief as long as other criteria are fulfilled, so that single fathers like himself needing domestic help will get the same relief as single women in his position?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, against the backdrop of geopolitical volatility, digitalisation and climate change, we are witnessing structural changes in the global economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Singapore’s growth and success are dependent on an open and global economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is Singapore strengthening our value proposition to address the risks and capture the opportunities driven by structural supply chain shifts to continue to anchor Singapore as a trusted and preferred hub for trade and business?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I will speak on Government procurement processes, focusing on quality discernment, support for SMEs and green procurement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our public officers must maintain the Government's stewardship role in securing the best quality at the right price.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does MOF ensure the effective and prudent use of public resources and how do we ensure that procurement policies are not only cost-effective but are synonymous with superior quality?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is imperative to equip our public officers with the skills and knowledge to discern quality and excellence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, local firms have provided feedback that the tender process has challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SMEs face difficulties in fulfilling track record requirements and meet minimum financial grading criteria for larger projects.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could the Ministry provide an update on the SME-lite tender scheme and how it is being refined based on feedback?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, how is the Government ensuring prompt payment to ease SMEs’ cash flow issues and, in circumstances where the SMEs are the subcontractors, how does the Government ensure that main contractors promptly pay the subcontractors?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What additional steps can MOF take to enhance the ease of business transactions with the Government?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How will initiatives like Invoice Now contribute to streamlining processes and what strategies are in place to expand its adoption across the private sector?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, how does MOF support companies in leveraging growth opportunities and fostering sustainability capabilities?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, one way to support local businesses and SMEs to build up their capabilities and track record is through Government tenders.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Industry groups have shared during my engagement with them that SMEs appreciate such opportunities, not just to increase revenues but also the chance to partner larger companies to sharpen their experience and learning.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While the Government has taken steps to reduce the administrative burden with new functions in GeBiz, such as an online repository, SMEs continue to feed back that accessibility and efficiency of Government tenders can be improved.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, SMEs highlighted how contract specifications may at times be too stringent to fulfil or too rigid to allow room for SMEs to propose more innovative solutions to address requirements.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They, therefore, hope contracts can be made more practical and flexible; while bundling and aggregation of contracts are logical, they could exclude smaller SMEs from bidding or compress their margins as they fulfil subcontracts with bigger SMEs as the middlemen; and startups, such as one specialising in AI video analytics which I met at the recent Singapore Airshow, asked whether the financial grading criteria can be eased to provide more opportunities for them to participate as vendors.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that most are asset-light with different risk profiles from traditional companies and they are still in the midst of building up their financial track record.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, the Government has outlined ambitious sustainability targets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What measures has the Government taken in its procurement policies to support and encourage suppliers of products and services to the Government to adopt more sustainable practices and grow their sustainability capabilities?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Are companies participating in the Government tenders able to meet the standards and requirements and the Government’s procurement considerations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Is the Government on track to achieve its green procurement goals?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What challenges has the Government encountered in its drive to green procurement?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, the green transition, inherently complex, necessitates a catalytic role from the Government.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It can help to mobilise funding and develop the right capabilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By offering incentives, providing regulatory support and fostering a conducive environment, the Government's intervention will be instrumental in making the green transition a reality.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the growing number of family offices in Singapore, philanthropy can be a promising avenue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With last year’s announcement of the Philanthropy Tax Incentive Scheme, philanthropy from Singapore is increasingly borderless and can be used to fund climate projects around the region.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This geographical flexibility will help boost the impact of philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must find ways to rapidly scale this impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We will see real sea change when the trillions in private capital can be effectively directed towards climate solutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, private investors, who seek financial returns, say there is still a lack of sufficient bankable, investable and fundable deal opportunities on the ground.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many projects are sub-scale and are too risky for private capital to access.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Innovative funding structures, such as blended finance, have been seen as a solution.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Under this initiative, together with MAS, development finance institutions and philanthropies could provide concessionary capital in the form of grants, limited guarantees and debt or equity at below market rates of return.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: On the basis that concessionary capital has been put together, this creates the conditions for banks and institutional investors to crowd in private and commercial capital.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When blended finance works well, the impact is significant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, the adoption of blended finance has been slow.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Blended finance often involves complex structuring to balance the risks and returns for different types of investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many blended finance projects are in new and emerging markets, with relatively few historical precedents to demonstrate their viability and potential for success.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This lack of proven track record can make investors hesitant to commit funds.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I therefore call on the Government to build awareness and understanding of blended finance amongst potential investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the net-zero goal will increasingly become a pre-requisite in the expectations of customers, investors as well as regulators across the world, it is urgent that we support our businesses to take action to stay competitive and relevant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies will increasingly be subjected to tighter sustainability reporting and regulations – particularly those with trading partners, such as those in the European Union, which have placed higher standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Government support to build a framework to help companies comply with reporting requirements and compliance practices that are required by their counterparties will be critical.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government's green procurement can significantly bolster green transition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By prioritising the purchase of eco-friendly and sustainable products and services, the Government sets a powerful precedent – encouraging suppliers to innovate and shift towards sustainable practices.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: This initiative – of paramount importance amongst the business community fearing the tight timeline might leave them unprepared, risking their compliance and operational continuity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Could MOF share insights into the extended milestones and how the Government plans to support companies – especially SMEs – through this change?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Mr Chairman, it cannot be gainsaid that philanthropy and volunteerism are key ingredients for building a strong social compact in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They foster our sense of togetherness, in addition to supplementing Government spending in funding social programmes and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: That is why we have traditionally offered generous tax deductions for cash donations made to Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs) for causes that benefit the local community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Corporate Volunteer Scheme – previously known as the Business & IPC Partnership Scheme – extended that tax benefit to corporates whose employees volunteer and provide services for IPCs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, I was quite surprised but also personally grateful, when Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the new Overseas Humanitarian Assistance Tax Deduction Scheme.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: There are many people elsewhere who are in greater need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Ultimately, regardless of the beneficiary, we can foster a culture of giving.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: What are the initiatives undertaken by MOF to strengthen our culture of giving and enable more people to contribute to our society?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Also, how do we monitor the approved list of overseas emergency humanitarian assistance causes?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Second Minister for Finance, Mr Chee Hong Tat.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions for MOF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, improving businesses' ease of transacting with Government and supporting their green transition; second, building a strong society together; third, strengthening Singapore's competitive advantage as a trusted hub for trade and enterprise; and fourth, effective and prudent use of public resources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will speak on the first two areas and Minister Indranee Rajah will cover the other two areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, we said that MOF will work with the business community to design Tender Lite – a new category of Government tender with fewer and simpler conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the past year, MOF has been engaging the Association of SMEs (ASME) and the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) to gather inputs from businesses to co-create Tender Lite together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have incorporated suggestions and inputs from our business leaders, to make Government contracts more accessible to SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we will share risks with businesses, while maintaining public accountability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will reduce the cost on the businesses and the risk they bear when taking part in Tender Lite tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also implemented the GeBIZ Supplier File Repository, which enables suppliers to upload their relevant business documents once – for use across multiple bids for all Government quotations and tenders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With the Repository, suppliers can save up to 5,000 hours in total across 100,000 bids submitted annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Derrick Goh asked if Government procurement could further support SMEs by giving preference to home-grown companies or to MNEs that partner with local SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a buyer, the Government needs to ensure prudent use of public funds by selecting cost-effective solutions that provide value-for-money outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our procurement rules are designed to achieve this in a fair and transparent way.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For many SMEs, Government contracts are an opportunity for them to build credibility and track record, which is helpful when they subsequently bid for private sector and overseas contracts; a point that Mr Goh mentioned too.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are able to achieve this because the buyers know that the Singapore Government awards contracts based on merit via open and fair competition – focusing on quality and value-for-money outcomes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our aim is to level the playing field and remove unnecessary obstacles that prevent competitive and innovative suppliers – including our small and new businesses – from participating in and winning Government contracts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, this is what we seek to do under Tender Lite and other initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, over 80% by number and about 40% by value of Government procurement opportunities have been awarded to SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is higher than the targets in Australia at 20% by value; and in China at 30% by value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also helping businesses reduce the cost of transacting with Government through eGuarantee@Gov, which is a simple and secure digital process for businesses and individuals to provide guarantees to Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since its launch in 2022, we have tripled the number of participating financial institutions and agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, we have around 60 participating financial institutions and 45 agencies and key regulatory processes across Government have been enhanced as a result.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, almost all guarantees submitted by businesses registering for import/export permits today, are now done through eGuarantee@Gov.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has reduced the time taken for the entire lodgement process of guarantees with Singapore Customs – from five working days to just one day.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses also benefit from not having to incur courier costs to deliver the physical guarantees to Customs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over 120,000 eGuarantees were issued to date and eGuarantee@Gov is expected to bring annual cost savings of around $600,000 to businesses, financial institutions and Government agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We target to expand eGuarantee@Gov to all Government agencies with guarantee needs by end 2024, which will lead to even greater savings opportunities for the entire ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, over 99% of the invoices billed to Government agencies adopt 30 days' or shorter credit terms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have committed to keep prompt payment rates above 95% and have consistently achieved this target.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In FY2022, 98% of invoices were paid within their credit terms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is comparable with the practices and commitment for prompt payments elsewhere, such as the UK and US.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To ensure that we maintain these standards, the Accountant-General's Department (AGD) monitors the prompt payments indicators regularly across the public sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We understand that businesses would prefer faster payments where possible to ease their cash flows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since 2021, the Government has been paying ahead of the credit terms for invoices below $5,000, after the receipt of goods or services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From April 2023 to January 2024, Ministries and Organs of State paid 98% of invoices – below $5,000 – ahead of their credit terms.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 85% of such invoices were paid to SMEs, benefitting over 15,000 of them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Then, we said, "As of end-January 2022, about 97% of e-invoices below $5,000 were paid within 12 days – ahead of the usual credit term of 30 days."   Sir, this is incorrect.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The average time taken to pay these invoices was about 12 days." Sir, there have been cases of incorrect billing and unsatisfactory delivery of goods and services by businesses – where invoices were rejected.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While such cases remain below 10% of all invoices, they do contribute to SMEs' concerns over cashflow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will work with our trade associations and chambers (TACs) – including SBF and ASME – as well as businesses to identify specific areas where we can enhance our processes and enable more businesses to receive payments promptly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Similar to what we have done by working together with our TACs and businesses on Tender Lite.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also study best practices from other countries and private-sector companies as part of our review.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Public sector agencies have also collaborated with one another to improve services to businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is the upcoming One-Stop Payroll initiative developed by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board and Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, employers need to use different systems to report an employees' income to IRAS for tax purposes – to CPF Board for payment of CPF and to report updates to employees' occupational and employment details to MOM.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The agencies got together to combine IRAS' existing Auto Inclusion Scheme seamless filing service with new filing services from the CPF Board and MOM, as an integrated digital solution offering.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One-Stop Payroll will enable businesses to use the same payroll software to submit annual payroll to IRAS and monthly CPF contribution data to CPF Board; and seamlessly update employees' occupational and employment details under MOM's Occupational Employment Dataset.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A win-win outcome which is good for businesses and good for our agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked how MOF is helping companies capture opportunities with the green transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The MTI will be addressing this at its COS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The support for businesses will also cover new requirements for sustainability reporting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2022, ACRA and the Singapore Exchange Regulation set up the industry-led Sustainability Reporting Advisory Committee (SRAC) to advise on a roadmap for climate reporting by companies in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The SRAC has made its recommendations and ACRA issued a public consultation last year to gather feedback.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has considered the public feedback carefully and will introduce mandatory climate disclosures in a phased approach – starting with listed companies, then larger non-listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other jurisdictions, such as the European Union, United Kingdom and New Zealand, have similarly introduced mandatory climate reporting requirements for both listed and non-listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ACRA will review in 2027 whether to extend the requirements to smaller non-listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have not made a decision on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ACRA will give companies sufficient notice before introducing any requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We recognise that some companies may have started climate reporting using different internationally recognised standards and frameworks to meet investors’ information needs and requirements of the jurisdictions that they operate in.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For such companies, we will provide a three-year transitional period during which we will exempt them from the new requirements, if they are using other internationally recognised standards and frameworks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Mark Lee asked about the timeline for mandating Scope 3 climate reporting disclosures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is better to take a phased approach, which I think Mr Lee will agree.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As for non-listed companies, we recognise that they need more time to build capabilities for Scope 3 disclosures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, we will not require non-listed companies, including large ones, to disclose Scope 3 emissions before FY2029.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will consider the industry's readiness and implementation experience from the listed companies before deciding when to require Scope 3 disclosures for non-listed companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Companies will be given at least two years' notice if the decision is to proceed with Scope 3 disclosures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government is also stepping up efforts to support large companies and SMEs through the green transition, including support to develop sustainability reporting and assurance competencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will elaborate on these support measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Edward Chia asked about policies to promote greener procurement practices by the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As buyers, our agencies are also encouraging and recognising the development of green capabilities by enterprises through green Government procurement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This helps our businesses build capabilities to meet the demands from consumers and investors for more sustainable products and supply chains.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, the Government has incorporated environmental sustainability considerations into our procurement and continuously reviewed our policies to procure greener solutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have implemented this for selected projects in 2023.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) set aside additional evaluation points for greener suppliers for a number of their tenders for the Cross Island Line, such as for Clementi station and King Albert Park station.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will take time for businesses to adjust to new sustainability considerations, so we are phasing these into Government tenders gradually, in consultation with the business community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are happy to see that companies participating in Government tenders are gradually adopting sustainability practices, such as disclosing their emissions and greening their operations and supply chains.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) will provide more details of the industry consultations and pilots.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although there are signs of improvement in the inflation situation, the Government is aware that our SMEs are very concerned with operating costs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence the Government will introduce various initiatives to help businesses reduce costs and simplify transaction processes between businesses and the Government, allowing businesses to save money, effort and time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also taken into account feedback from businesses and introduced a series of platforms to reduce the administrative cost for businesses and make transactions more convenient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These include eGuarantee@Gov, which allows businesses to quickly provide bank guarantees or risks guarantees to government agencies and a one-stop system to report employee income: One-Stop Payroll.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Apart from assisting businesses in reducing costs, the Government will also help them to expand their business capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In this regard, we will work with businesses to advance the transition towards sustainable development and acquire new skills in digital economy and environmental sustainability, thereby enhancing their competitiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will continue to take a multi-pronged approach to build an efficient and sustainable pro-business environment, to actively support businesses in their development and transformation. : Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions on taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Mark Lee asked whether MOF could broaden the definition of qualifying IP for corporate tax purposes, and whether the IP development tax incentive could be enhanced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government supports businesses to leverage IP for their growth through various tax and non-tax measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Enterprises may tap on Government grant schemes administered by Enterprise Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Singapore IP Strategy 2030 was also launched three years ago to strengthen Singapore’s position as a global intangible assets and IP hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In parallel, our corporate income tax regime also provides support through various schemes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The scope of qualifying IP for our tax schemes broadly follows the definition used by the World Intellectual Property Organization, as well as international tax standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF will continue to review our schemes for relevance, with careful consideration of their costs, benefits and consistency with international standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked how MOF considers when to raise the chargeable personal income tax threshold for the lowest tiers, as well as the $1 million threshold for GST registration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has taken steps to address cost-of-living concerns, especially for lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned some of these during the Budget Debate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Among those who do pay personal income tax, 80% of them have an effective tax rate of less than 6%.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The vast majority of income taxes are paid by the top 10% of taxpayers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We review the personal income tax regime from time to time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We raised the top marginal tax rates in recent years and have just announced an increase in the annual income threshold for dependant-related reliefs from $4,000 to $8,000 this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF will continue to review the regime, including the exemption threshold, and ensure that it remains competitive, progressive and fiscally-resilient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It was set very high to exempt most SMEs from the additional costs necessary to comply with GST collection requirements; around 90% of businesses in 1994 were exempted from having to register from GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At that time, the UK VAT registration threshold was just £45,000, which is about S$75,000, while Australia’s was A$50,000, or S$45,000, when they introduced GST in 2000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And our threshold remains significantly higher than in most other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, the UK’s threshold now is £85,000, or about S$145,000, while Australia’s threshold is now A$75,000, or about S$65,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, around 70% of businesses that newly register for GST today do so voluntarily, even though their turnover falls below the threshold.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to assess the appropriateness of this threshold as part of our regular policy reviews.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about extending the Foreign Domestic Worker Levy Relief (FDWLR) to divorced single working fathers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He explained that this was because we already have a migrant domestic worker levy concession, which provides more targeted support for families who need help caring for their dependants, regardless of whether they pay income tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes single working fathers with young children living in the same household.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They can qualify for the migrant domestic worker levy concession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to implement comprehensive support measures to address the concerns of Singaporeans and foster an enabling and supportive ecosystem for community giving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is key to helping us build a strong social compact, and a caring and cohesive society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong explained, we apply monetary policy levers to temper imported inflation, and fiscal policy to further cushion the impact of inflation on Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We enhanced the Assurance Package in Budget 2024 to provide near-term relief, as we think this is needed even as inflation moderates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the Government deploys these measures, we actively monitor the impact and we are prepared to do more to support Singaporeans should it become necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we will do so in a manner which is fair, effective and sustainable, for both current and future generations, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa said earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also been actively strengthening our enabling ecosystem for mutual support, and this helps forge a strong and united society that progresses together as one people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF provides various forms of support for community giving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out, we provide various tax deductions schemes – for qualifying donations made to Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs), for corporate volunteering, and for qualifying overseas donations towards emergency humanitarian assistance causes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Beyond tax deductions, we also support charitable giving through Government matching grants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, during the challenging COVID-19 period, we enhanced our support for charities through Tote Board’s Enhanced Fundraising Programme which provides dollar-for-dollar matching for eligible donations received by charities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A key ingredient in building a strong society is partnership.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When we harness the expertise, experience and passions of diverse stakeholders and combine our efforts to serve our community, this can create a ripple effect and lead to a sustained positive impact on our society.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has brought together the People, Private and Public sectors to support community and ground-up initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a key element of Forward Singapore – individuals and corporates stepping up to work together on challenges facing our society and to care for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another initiative – called BAGUS Together – was launched in January this year by Tote Board, Temasek Foundation and the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre to strengthen our groundup ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: BAGUS Together – which stands for Building All Groundups for Success Together – will rally funders, corporates and volunteers to support groundups in their journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will provide groundups access to critical resources and networks to enable them to deliver stronger and more sustained community impact.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Groundups play an integral role in meeting the needs of local communities and particular groups that are not easily catered for with broad-based programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, this is why we want to support them.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And, this is where BAGUS Together can come in as a first-stop platform to connect changemakers with a community of skilled volunteers and like-minded partners to share resources, grow capabilities and support one another's efforts to create a positive impact on our community.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Government ensures effective and prudent use of public resources, including for spending needs that span several years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We seek to achieve prudent spending with good outcomes, that is, value for money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Based on 2022 OECD data, general government expenditure in other advanced economies, such as the UK, Korea and Germany, exceeded 40% of GDP, while that of Switzerland was about 30% of GDP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As our spending needs rise, we will continue to manage our expenditure growth carefully.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have mechanisms to evaluate our spending and to reallocate resources across the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Aside from prudent spending, at the macro level, we also constantly strive to optimise our spending.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, for large expenditure items, such as major infrastructure projects, MOF applies additional scrutiny to evaluate their worthiness and cost effectiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Larger-scale and more complex projects are also reviewed by the Development Projects Advisory Panel, comprising experts from across the private and public sectors and academia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is in addition to agencies' own efforts to ensure cost-effective infrastructure spending when they are developing their designs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) considers rail alignment, site and ground conditions in determining the appropriate tunnelling design for our Mass Rapid Transit system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, Government programmes are subject to evaluation and reviews to ensure that their purposes are met.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where relevant, the findings also inform how these programmes can be refined to enhance their effectiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, a study commissioned by the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) showed that parents and caregivers who received KidSTART home visits had more positive interactions with their children than families who did not receive such support and these children also showed improved socio-emotional development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a result, the revised KidSTART model will deliver child development interventions mainly through home visits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Government agencies also constantly re-engineer their processes and digitalise them for greater effectiveness and efficiency.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Accountant-General's Department digitalised audit workflows across the public sector through the Audit and Governance Enterprise Management System to enable timely identification, analysis and remediation of audit issues across the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The public sector is committed to ensuring that our processes are kept lean and efficient, while providing ample guidance and ensuring sound governance for public offices to respond in an agile and nimble manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Jessica Tan also asked how MOF is strengthening our competitiveness and hub status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Through decades of hard work, we have built an international reputation as a reliable and trusted hub for business and trade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A key enabler is to have a strong and robust accountancy and audit ecosystem.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Accountants play a vital role in safeguarding and supporting businesses, and Singapore's strong accounting sector has been the bedrock of our trusted business hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But the sector has faced manpower challenges in recent years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Fewer students are enrolling in accounting degrees and among the graduates, fewer are pursuing accounting-related careers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF set up the Accountancy Workforce Review Committee (AWRC) in 2022 to study these challenges and see how we can build a sustainable pipeline of local accountancy talent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The AWRC's work is almost completed and the Committee expects to issue its recommendations in the coming months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In line with the AWRC deliberations, the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) and the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA), have expanded the pathways for Singaporeans to consider accountancy as a career and obtain the necessary professional qualifications and experience to practise as an accountant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some of the programme's requirements will also be streamlined while maintaining rigour and quality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF and ACRA have also been galvanising stakeholders to support the AWRC's work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) recently launched a new four-year Bachelor of Accountancy in Sustainability Management and Analytics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This builds on NTU's existing three-year Bachelor of Accountancy programme with new features, such as a 30-week internship component, for practical industry exposure and opportunities to work or study overseas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Through these, students will be able to accumulate more work experience and career development opportunities earlier, and enjoy an accelerated pathway to becoming a chartered accountant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I am confident that our partnership efforts with stakeholders will strengthen the accountancy sector and, in turn, Singapore's position as a trusted business hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Another key competitive advantage of our business hub is our pro-business, pro-trade stance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MOF continually works to enhance our trade processes to facilitate the flow of goods and reduce regulatory costs for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore Customs has played a leading role in developing the Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA), signed by all ASEAN member states.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The MRA will recognise each member state's authorised economic operators (AEOs).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under this arrangement, the AEO companies will enjoy faster documentary and cargo clearance for movement of goods within ASEAN.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This saves time and money and shortens the time for goods to reach market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is our first multilateral MRA and adds to the 12 bilateral MRAs we already have with other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As trade with ASEAN member states accounts for a significant 28% of our trade in goods, this will benefit many businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: By improving and streamlining our trade processes, we are also strengthening Singapore's position as a global trade node.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We cannot take Singapore's hub status for granted and I urge all stakeholders to work with our businesses and help them acquire new capabilities and be more competitive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked whether the Government has over-resourced the Merdeka Generation Fund and may be doing likewise for the Majulah Package Fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Let us first start with the principle underpinning our approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For large commitments like the Merdeka Generation (MG) Package, we set aside resources as and when we can to meet our commitment to every single one of our MG seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was based on projections of spending and life expectancy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the four years since 2019, we have disbursed $0.9 billion from the fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, we have concurrently earned investment and interest income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, the net drawdown is $0.4 billion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This can be found on page 79 of the Government Financial Statements. $5.7 billion is less than what we would need to meet our remaining commitment to the MG seniors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is at page 78 of the Government Financial Statements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is more than the $5.7 billion remaining in the fund.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to carefully monitor healthcare utilisation and longevity trends, and make top-ups in future, if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leong then had several other miscellaneous questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: His questions can be categorised into two groups: one, on revenue; and the other group on some specific expenditure items.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In relation to the first group, I think he suggested that we had not provided sufficient information on taxes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Actually, the information is already available in the Revenue and Expenditure Estimates – also known as the Budget Book – which can also be used for weightlifting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He said that we did not explain what "Other Taxes" were.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Actually, this can be found in the Overview of the Budget Book at page XIX, which tells you what the "Other Taxes" comprise, which essentially include Foreign Worker Levy, Water Conservation Tax, Land Betterment Charge and the Annual Tonnage Tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And it is also on page XX; and it is in the footnote of page XX; and it is again on page XXI and it is also elaborated there.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And again, it is on page XXII; and there is a further footnote at page XXII.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, actually, we explained what the "Other Taxes" were not once, not twice, not three times; but four times inside the Budget Book.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leong also asked for the reasons that we collected higher revenue on Other Taxes and Corporate Income Tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The reasons can be found in the Analysis of Revenue and Expenditure, which was published on the same day as the Budget Book and can be found on the MOF website.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Very briefly, the FY2023 estimates for Other Taxes were revised upwards because of higher Land Betterment Charge collections from unforeseen redevelopment projects, and the increase in the FY2023 estimates for Corporate Income Tax was due to stronger-than-expected economic growth in 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, now let me deal with the second group of questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On Electronic Road Pricing (ERP), the revenue estimates are reported under the C16 Account: Transport and Communication, Licence and Permits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For both FY2023 and FY2024, ERP collections are estimated to be about $80 million annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Based on actual collections from January to December 2023, Work Permit and S Pass holders accounted for around 77% and 17% of total collections respectively, with the rest attributable to Migrant Domestic Workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, it would include commercial properties as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, there are about 33 seconds left.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would only need maybe a couple more minutes to complete.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think there is some extra time for me, if I may complete the reply.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have got up to 6.50 pm, so please proceed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More generally, any report, including the Budget Book, presents data in meaningful ways for its users.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, not every single tax, fee, line item expenditure or capital receipt is listed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can imagine how many more pages the Budget Book would need to have if that were to be the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We therefore aggregate smaller items into larger groupings in our reporting and highlight the more salient changes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moving on to expenditure, some of these cuts would have been better addressed by other Ministries.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nonetheless, since Mr Leong has raised them, I will touch on them briefly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On SPH Media Trust, the Minister for Communications and Information will share more at MCI’s COS.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On HDB’s deficit, it is on the books of HDB, which is a Statutory Board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, information on HDB’s deficit can be found in HDB’s Financial Statements, rather than the Revenue and Expenditure Estimates.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: FY2023 and FY2024 information will be published in due course.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With regard to Ministers travelling overseas for official appointments in their private capacities, this information is not tracked as a separate item of expenditure.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, it is important to understand that Ministers taking up international appointments in their private capacities are allowed to do so only when it is in the interest or in the service of the nation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, in those situations, they are travelling and working on behalf of the state, albeit in their private capacity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, they are doing it for the state even though they are using their private capacity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is not a case where it is the state funding their own personal things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are allowed to do this because it is in the interest of the state that they do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, it would be part and parcel of the normal expenditure that you would expect and it comes under the expenses reflected in two accounts, "2100 Consumption of Products and Services" and "2400 International and Public Relations, Public Communications", on page 8 of the Budget Book.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In any case, there are very few who have done so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I should also say that when the few Ministers travel in the private capacity, do not forget when they go there, they may well also have official meetings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In fact, to save time, very often, we would do that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, one trip may serve multiple purposes, some in their official capacity and then, one or two meetings in their private capacity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The focus of providing these spending figures is for accountability of spending on these projects.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the total project cost and annual spending of each development project is listed in the Budget Book, Mr Leong can look these up, based on his area of interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And finally, regarding capital injections into Temasek Holdings, Mr Leong previously filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on this topic in January last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, MOF is committed to ensuring fiscal sustainability, prudent spending and achieving good value-for-money outcomes for the benefit of current and future generations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let us continue to work in partnership to build a strong, united, and inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: To Minister Indranee, pertaining to the Singapore Chartered Accountancy Qualifications or SCAQ, on behalf of ISCA, I thank MOF for making improvements to the Singapore Chartered Accountancy Qualifications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: We shared these improvements to the IHLs last week.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think we can certainly bring the attention of the SCAQ not just to civil servants but to everyone who is looking to come into the accountancy sector, looking to upskill, upgrade and find new career pathways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the accountancy sector comes under MOF, so we would recommend it in general.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: I am glad to hear about the Government's ambition to be an IP hub.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: First, some businesses have patented IPs but prefer not to officially register to safeguard sensitive information, like formula and proprietary knowledge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Will the Government actually consider expanding the IP Development Tax Incentive to cover this?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: Second, I think IP valuation is both an art and a science.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee
text: In our pursuit of being an IP hub for the region, what are the Government's plans in building this talent base?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Mark Lee for his questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To his first question, we will take a look at the specific suggestion that Mr Lee has brought up.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I just want to go back to what I mentioned in my speech earlier, that MOF, when we review some of these schemes, we have to take a look at the cost benefit but also to check on consistency with international standards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think this is important because at the end of the day, we do need to also make sure that our standards that we apply here are consistent with international standards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to Mr Lee's second question, certainly this is a very important area under the Singapore IP Strategy 2030, because if you do not have a talent pipeline, you cannot execute and implement many of the good ideas.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think the Ministry of Law will elaborate on this during their COS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Minister for the detailed reply to the various questions, when I asked for more details on the estimates.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, I would like to ask on the Other Taxes, even in the Budget Book, it did not break down the Foreign Worker Levy, Water Conservation Tax and Land Betterment Charge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Essentially, as I mentioned earlier in my reply, you would give as much information as is necessary for people looking at the Budget Book to use it meaningfully, but you do not go down into — you have got line item, then every single one, then you go down further and further and further.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There comes a point where the degree of granularity does not really serve as much of a useful purpose when you are considering the Revenue and Expenditure Estimates for an entire financial year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, basically, the information that is provided in the Budget Book is very similar to what is provided in many other countries and the purpose, of course, is to allow people to see what the Revenue and Expenditure Estimates are like, and for Parliament to be able to debate and decide on the financial policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I mean, I just want to confirm that that is the case, that that is the way we are treating the accounts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But for today's purposes and in my response, because you must remember that the initial cut was that we did not explain what these other taxes were and that we did not give a breakdown of the taxes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, hence, my reply was that we have given a breakdown of the taxes because we told you exactly what they are.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Chairman, okay, I will let the matter rest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But before that, my question actually specifically asks for a breakdown of these taxes, but okay, we let the matter rest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are just talking about I think today and over the whole process of the Budget debate, one of the key themes that we were talking about is transparency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We hope that we can get more data and information so that we can understand the whole Budget process better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And over the years – this is my fourth Budget debate – I found that there are actually many information that is still lacking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I just have one question left for the Minister and that is in view of what I said just now, to increase the amount of information that we can get, there are three areas at least I do not know whether the Government can commit to offer to us going forward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that MOF had come up with the medium-term fiscal projections last year, but the whole report is actually very brief.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Going forward, can we offer more details as to how the analysis is being done, what are the basic data and all those details and things?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have seen a lot of financial reports in the course of my career.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I would say that by the standard I know, the medium-term fiscal projections report is very brief.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is like you want us to just take the conclusion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I think we need to know the analysis behind it.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Leong, may I invite you to ask your questions?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, the question is whether going forward, MOF can provide us with more detailed fiscal projections, spending and revenue projection, one?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: How do you decide what amount you want to put in, the expected payout and all those things?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think that would allow us to understand the whole budget process better.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because right now, it seems that there is a budget process and there is also an off-budget process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: All the money is in the endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So all this I think would help us a lot going forward, to understand better about how we have used our money.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Leong for his further clarifications.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are lots of different items and the question is what level of detail do you need?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We adhere to the same general standards, so it is the same level of transparency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then the second question that he raised was for the medium-term fiscal projections.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Leong says that he has seen lots of other financial documents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They may be documents of companies, but financial documents of other countries?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When you look at a country – that is very different from reporting like a company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The volume, the business, the things that a country has to look at and the Ministries, the items are huge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, what you do is you put forward projections in a way that gives sort of a meaningful direction; it sets out the Government's thrust; it sets out the key items or things that you think you will have to deal with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the Member has questions or queries, then of course the Member can file questions and then that will be answered at the appropriate time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I was not quite sure I understood the thrust of that projection on the endowment and the other funds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that, I think was dealt with by Deputy Prime Minister earlier.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, may I invite you to withdraw your cut?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And also for their continuing assurance to Singaporeans to cope with the current cost situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I also want to thank Minister Indranee and Minister Chee Hong Tat for their comprehensive reply.
